faq.q: What if a patient cannot afford methotrexate?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with morning stiffness >2 h and symmetrical hand swelling. What is the next best step? — Obtain RF and anti‑CCP; if positive, start methotrexate.
A patient on methotrexate develops elevated liver enzymes. What do you do? — Stop methotrexate, repeat LFTs in 2 weeks, consider switching to hydroxychloroquine.

A 45‑year‑old man with RA has a new cough and fever. What is the differential? — Pulmonary involvement of RA, infection (TB, pneumonia), or drug‑induced lung disease. Order chest X‑ray and sputum tests.
Why is anti‑CCP more specific than RF? — Anti‑CCP targets citrullinated peptides unique to RA, whereas RF can be positive in other autoimmune diseases.
A patient cannot afford methotrexate. Which DMARD is a reasonable alternative? — Hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine, though efficacy is lower.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in patients with renal impairment? — They can worsen kidney function and increase bleeding risk.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune synovitis that presents with symmetrical polyarthritis, often of small joints. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria, serology and imaging, while management focuses on disease‑modifying drugs and supportive care adapted to resource limits.

sections.p: RA is a systemic autoimmune disease characterised by chronic synovial inflammation leading to joint destruction. The 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria combine joint involvement, serology, acute‑phase reactants and symptom duration.
Disease activity is staged by DAS28 or simplified scores, guiding treatment intensity. In low‑resource settings, a clinical DAS28‑CRP (≥2.6 active, <2.6 remission) is practical.
Genetic predisposition (HLA‑DRB1 shared epitope) plus environmental triggers such as smoking, infections (e.g., streptococcal pharyngitis) and chronic inflammation.

Patients report morning stiffness >1 hour, swelling of metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, symmetrical pain, and fatigue. Extra‑articular features may include nodules and lung involvement.
Use affordable tests: CBC, ESR/CRP, RF, anti‑CCP, basic X‑ray. When unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and ESR.
Look for rapidly destructive joints, severe pain unresponsive to NSAIDs, fever, weight loss, or pulmonary infiltrates. Complications include osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and infections.

Treat the underlying inflammation with disease‑modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). In low‑resource settings, methotrexate is first line; hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine are alternatives. NSAIDs provide symptomatic relief.

t.b: Avoid if liver disease or pregnancy
Avoid in renal impairment or peptic ulcer

sections.p: Regular clinical review every 3–6 months, monitor disease activity, adjust DMARDs, and screen for osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk. Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.
Seronegative spondyloarthritis, osteoarthritis, and septic arthritis can mimic RA.
RF can be positive in other autoimmune diseases; anti‑CCP is more specific. ESR may be normal in early RA or in patients on steroids.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain not relieved by NSAIDs
